stops.date_confidence: the date is agreed everywhere; the place is not. Modern consensus gives Stuttgart: en.wikipedia's infobox reads 'Died: 30 June 1522 (aged 67), Stuttgart, Duchy of Wuerttemberg', and de.wikipedia agrees. The nineteenth-century reference works give Liebenzell: the ADB states plainly that he died at Bad Liebenzell, and the Jewish Encyclopedia has him dying 'at Liebenzell, near Hirschau, Wuerttemberg'. This is modern encyclopaedias against nineteenth-century ones, not two coequal traditions, and it is recorded rather than resolved. The pin is the Leonhardskirche, where the burial is not in dispute

stops.stop: Worms, standing on the wall of the Luther monument
stops.date_confidence: attested that Reuchlin appears on the Lutherdenkmal at Worms, and that he is a full standing statue on the monument's surrounding wall rather than a relief: de.wikipedia, 'Lutherdenkmal (Worms)' places him there alongside Melanchthon, Frederick the Wise, and Philip the Magnanimous, with Luther central and Waldes, Wyclif, Hus, and Savonarola below. No date for the figure was established in this research; 1868 is used only to order the posthumous stops and is not asserted

stops.segment: The Stone on the Choir Wall
stops.stop: Stuttgart, the church in ruins and the stone brought back
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Leonhardskirche was severely damaged in the Stuttgart raid of 22 August 1944 and rebuilt 1948-1954 under Rudolf Lempp, and that the gravestone survived and is displayed on the choir wall with an 1871 portrait medallion (de.wikipedia, 'Leonhardskirche (Stuttgart)'). de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin' gives 1955 for the move of the stone into the church; the church's own article dates the rebuilding to 1954 and does not name 1955, an unresolved date contradiction between two pages recorded here and not adjudicated. No day is recorded

stops.segment: The Stone on the Choir Wall
stops.stop: Pforzheim, the prize on the five-hundredth birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia, 'Reuchlinpreis' gives the foundation by the city of Pforzheim in 1955 on the five-hundredth anniversary of his birth, for outstanding German-language humanities scholarship, awarded roughly biennially with the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences, with Gershom Scholem among the laureates in 1969 and Hans-Georg Gadamer in 1971. The 1922 Barlach medal is attested on de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin'; the claim that en.wikipedia carries it is wrong, that article having no commemoration section at all. Scholem's reported remarks in 1969 crediting Reuchlin with helping begin the scholarly study of Judaism are summarized secondhand and the acceptance speech itself was not located, so that attribution is [R]

stops.segment: The Stone on the Choir Wall
stops.stop: Pforzheim, the Reuchlinhaus in the Stadtgarten
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia, 'Reuchlinhaus' gives construction 1957-1961 to a 1953 design by Manfred Lehmbruck, on the site of an earlier hall of 1900-1945 destroyed in the bombing, now housing the Schmuckmuseum and the Kunstverein. The statue by Matthias Daempfle is placed in the Stadtgarten by de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin', while de.wikipedia, 'Pforzheim' refers to a Reuchlin statue am Schlossberg: an internal conflict within German Wikipedia, recorded and not resolved. The Goethe couplet is traceable to a named text, the Zahme Xenien, book V, and is quoted in full on de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin'; the claim that en.wikipedia carries the Wunderzeichen phrase is wrong
